ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the institutional review board of National Tsing Hua University under number 11204HT041 and complied with ethical standards for research involving human participants.

To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs).
Participants were excluded if they were aged over 30 years, male, or had incomplete recordings, resulting in a final sample of 21 nonsmoking female university students (M = 18.99 years, SD = 1.17).
Accordingly, participants were classified as meditation-naïve with respect to formal and sustained meditation training.
Each participant completed 13 sessions corresponding to different audio conditions, with each session explicitly conducted on a separate day.

Following each session, participants completed self-report questionnaires in approximately 3-5 minutes, whereas the health status assessment and demographic questionnaire were required only at the first session.

In phase 1, participants were instructed to close their eyes, shift attention to bodily sensations, refrain from deliberate thinking, gently move their shoulders up and down to release tension, relax their abdomens, and rest in a relaxed state.

In phase 2, participants were guided to focus attention on the tip of the nose and observe natural, voluntary breathing while silently counting breaths, thereby engaging in a breathing-focused practice.

Pre-and post-intervention systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and pulse rate (PR) were measured using an Omron HEM-1000 upper arm blood pressure monitor while participants were seated with both feet flat on the floor.
Participants completed the following self-report measures.

Participants completed two single-item assessments of health status using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very poor to5 = excellent): (1) "Over the past month, how would you rate your psychological health?"
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To definitively address this gap, the present study implemented an unprecedented highdensity, within-subject experimental design. An a priori power analysis confirmed robust statistical power for this intensive repeated-measures approach (Faul et al., 2007). By exposing a tightly controlled cohort of 21 meditation-naïve females to 13 distinct, computationally engineered acoustic variations of a standardized 4-minute and 5-second breathing meditation, we successfully generated a massive dataset of 273 high-density physiological observation epochs. To precisely isolate the acute physiological reflexes driven by acoustic stimuli, eliminating baseline biological noise was paramount. We purposefully restricted our cohort to a homogenous group of 21 meditation-naïve females. Rather than a limitation, this stringent restriction served as a vital control strategy against sex-hormonal and age-related autonomic variance. Combined with a highly intensive within-subject design across 13 separate days, this approach yielded 273 high-density observation epochs, allowing us to map pure, unconfounded bioacoustic autonomic modulations.

An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for a repeated-measures within-subject design. To detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25) with an alpha level of .05 and a statistical power of .80 across 13 distinct audio measurements, a minimum of 19 participants was required. To rigorously isolate the nuanced physiological effects and eliminate sex-related cardiovascular variance, the sample was purposefully restricted to healthy, meditation-naïve females. The final sample of 21 participants successfully completed all 13 high-density recording sessions, yielding a massive dataset of 273 physiological observation epochs. This intensive sampling density provided exceptionally robust statistical power for the within-subject analyses, allowing for the precise detection of micro-level autonomic shifts driven by acoustic variations.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .01", Text = "Blue shading indicates the significance level of the corresponding effect: light blue, p < .05; middle blue, p < .01; dark blue, p < .001."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: Breathing guidance significantly reduced SBP (F (1, 20)= 14.200, p = <.001) and DBP (F (1, 20)= 7.211, p = .014), but not PR (F (1, 20)= 3.559, p = .074).
table.header: Three acoustically distinct clusters were identified among the 13 audio conditions.
table.expanded: Breathing guidance significantly reduced SBP (F (1, 20)= 14.200, p = <.001) and DBP (F (1, 20)= 7.211, p = .014), but not PR (F (1, 20)= 3.559, p = .074).

table.header: Associations with acoustic features were observed for most biosignal indices except respiration.
table.expanded: Subjective audio feeling did not differ significantly across audio groups (F(1.364, 27.288) = .258, p = .689) for the full audio.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .074", "p = .689"), Sentence = c("Breathing guidance significantly reduced SBP (F (1, 20)= 14.200, p = <.001) and DBP (F (1, 20)= 7.211, p = .014), but not PR (F (1, 20)= 3.559, p = .074).", "Subjective audio feeling did not differ significantly across audio groups (F(1.364, 27.288) = .258, p = .689) for the full audio." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs).
Participants were excluded if they were aged over 30 years, male, or had incomplete recordings, resulting in a final sample of 21 nonsmoking female university students (M = 18.99 years, SD = 1.17).
Accordingly, participants were classified as meditation-naïve with respect to formal and sustained meditation training.
Each participant completed 13 sessions corresponding to different audio conditions, with each session explicitly conducted on a separate day.

Following each session, participants completed self-report questionnaires in approximately 3-5 minutes, whereas the health status assessment and demographic questionnaire were required only at the first session.

In phase 1, participants were instructed to close their eyes, shift attention to bodily sensations, refrain from deliberate thinking, gently move their shoulders up and down to release tension, relax their abdomens, and rest in a relaxed state.

In phase 2, participants were guided to focus attention on the tip of the nose and observe natural, voluntary breathing while silently counting breaths, thereby engaging in a breathing-focused practice.

Pre-and post-intervention systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and pulse rate (PR) were measured using an Omron HEM-1000 upper arm blood pressure monitor while participants were seated with both feet flat on the floor.
Participants completed the following self-report measures.

Participants completed two single-item assessments of health status using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very poor to5 = excellent): (1) "Over the past month, how would you rate your psychological health?"
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation.

report: #### MATLAB code, no reproducible output

13 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run `diary('output.txt')` (or `diary on`) before the analysis and `diary off` after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use `publish('script.m', 'pdf')` (or the Live Editor's Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

text.text: While digital health platforms increasingly deliver guided mindful breathing interventions via audio, the specific acoustic properties of the guidance are fundamentally ignored as potential active ingredients.

This within-subject study implemented an unprecedented high-density experimental design to investigate how distinct, computationally engineered acoustic features (e.g., pitch, zero-crossing rate, natural background sounds) modulate acute cardiovascular, respiratory, and autonomic responses.

To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs).
Multiparametric biosignals, including pulse rate variability (PRV), respiratory dynamics, and electrodermal activity (EDA), were continuously recorded.
Results demonstrated a robust reduction in blood pressure independent of audio conditions, confirming the fundamental efficacy of a single bout of spontaneous breath awareness.

However, high-resolution analyses revealed a highly modular architecture where peripheral autonomic indices (EDA and PRV) were acutely sensitive to fine-grained acoustic features, specifically Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs).
Furthermore, physiological coupling patterns reorganized dynamically depending strictly on the acoustic context.

These findings fundamentally challenge the assumption that meditation audio is a neutral delivery medium, establishing acoustic parameters as potent, independent modulators of human autonomic reflexes for future digital therapeutics.
When we listen to a guided meditation on a smartphone to relieve stress, what exactly is calming our nervous system?

While the efficacy of a single 5-minute bout of short-term mindful breathing is well-established (Balban et al., 2023; Electrophysiology, 1996; Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017), the exponential growth of computer-assisted interventions persists in a critical oversight.
text.formatted: While the efficacy of a single 5-minute bout of short-term mindful breathing is well-established <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Balban et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Electrophysiology, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017)</ref>, the exponential growth of computer-assisted interventions persists in a critical oversight.

text.text: Grounded in Polyvagal Theory (Porges, 2011), the human autonomic nervous system is evolutionarily wired to respond to specific acoustic frequencies, bypassing conscious cognition to directly regulate physiological arousal.
text.formatted: Grounded in Polyvagal Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Porges, 2011)</ref>, the human autonomic nervous system is evolutionarily wired to respond to specific acoustic frequencies, bypassing conscious cognition to directly regulate physiological arousal.

text.text: However, current digital health frameworks universally treat audio guidance merely as a neutral vehicle for cognitive instruction, profoundly disregarding how the computational acoustic envelope itself acts as a digital active ingredient.

This oversight contrasts sharply with the recently proposed Sonic One Health framework (Pijanowski et al., 2025), which conceptualizes the acoustic environment not merely as a passive backdrop but as a dynamic pathway of exposure that actively drives outcomes across biological systems.
text.formatted: This oversight contrasts sharply with the recently proposed Sonic One Health framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Pijanowski et al., 2025)</ref>, which conceptualizes the acoustic environment not merely as a passive backdrop but as a dynamic pathway of exposure that actively drives outcomes across biological systems.

text.text: Current digital health frameworks implicitly treat audio guidance as a neutral delivery vehicle, fundamentally disregarding how the computational acoustic envelope itself acts as a digital active ingredient capable of directly innervating the autonomic nervous system.
Recent neurophysiological evidence shows that even a single bout of short-term structured respiration can rapidly reduce physiological arousal (Balban et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recent neurophysiological evidence shows that even a single bout of short-term structured respiration can rapidly reduce physiological arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Balban et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, current digital health frameworks implicitly treat audio guidance merely as a "dumb pipe", a neutral vehicle for delivering cognitive instructions.
This assumption fundamentally disregards the power of sound itself to bypass conscious processing and elicit direct neurophysiological reflexes.

In the field of bioacoustics, specific computational features, such as the zero-crossing rate (ZCR), spectral centroid, and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), are wellestablished metrics of auditory perception and emotional expression (Mitrović et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In the field of bioacoustics, specific computational features, such as the zero-crossing rate (ZCR), spectral centroid, and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), are wellestablished metrics of auditory perception and emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mitrović et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Wang et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Variations in vocal pitch and ambient noise are intricately linked to a listener's autonomic states (Zhao et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Variations in vocal pitch and ambient noise are intricately linked to a listener's autonomic states <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Zhao et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If we are to fully understand the mechanistic pathways of mind-body interventions and design environments that optimize human wellbeing, we must first deconstruct this blind spot.
It is imperative to determine whether finegrained acoustic properties, the acoustic essence of the soundscape, independently drive peripheral autonomic tone during a standardized behavioral task.
To definitively address this gap, the present study implemented an unprecedented highdensity, within-subject experimental design.
An a priori power analysis confirmed robust statistical power for this intensive repeated-measures approach (Faul et al., 2007).
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis confirmed robust statistical power for this intensive repeated-measures approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: By exposing a tightly controlled cohort of 21 meditation-naïve females to 13 distinct, computationally engineered acoustic variations of a standardized 4-minute and 5-second breathing meditation, we successfully generated a massive dataset of 273 high-density physiological observation epochs.
To precisely isolate the acute physiological reflexes driven by acoustic stimuli, eliminating baseline biological noise was paramount.
We purposefully restricted our cohort to a homogenous group of 21 meditation-naïve females.
Rather than a limitation, this stringent restriction served as a vital control strategy against sex-hormonal and age-related autonomic variance.

Combined with a highly intensive within-subject design across 13 separate days, this approach yielded 273 high-density observation epochs, allowing us to map pure, unconfounded bioacoustic autonomic modulations.

We hypothesized that while the core cognitive task of breath awareness would yield generalized cardiovascular reductions, the complex interactions among multiparametric biosignals, including respiratory dynamics, pulse rate variability (PRV), and electrodermal activity (EDA), would be distinctly and independently driven by the computational acoustic parameters of the digital stimulus.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for a repeated-measures within-subject design.
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> for a repeated-measures within-subject design.

text.text: To detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25) with an alpha level of .05 and a statistical power of .80 across 13 distinct audio measurements, a minimum of 19 participants was required.
To rigorously isolate the nuanced physiological effects and eliminate sex-related cardiovascular variance, the sample was purposefully restricted to healthy, meditation-naïve females.
The final sample of 21 participants successfully completed all 13 high-density recording sessions, yielding a massive dataset of 273 physiological observation epochs.

This intensive sampling density provided exceptionally robust statistical power for the within-subject analyses, allowing for the precise detection of micro-level autonomic shifts driven by acoustic variations.
This study used a within-subject repeated-measures design across 13 audio sessions.
The study initially recruited 38 university students.
Participants were excluded if they were aged over 30 years, male, or had incomplete recordings, resulting in a final sample of 21 nonsmoking female university students (M = 18.99 years, SD = 1.17).
The majority of participants reported no alcohol consumption (76.19%), and 57.14% reported engaging in regular exercise.
None of the participants reported a regular meditation practice during the three months prior to participation.
Although a small proportion reported limited prior exposure to meditation-related learning, the average duration of such experience was less than one year (M = .29 years, SD = .70).
Accordingly, participants were classified as meditation-naïve with respect to formal and sustained meditation training.
Detailed descriptions are publicly available online (https://osf.io/47z8a/overview?view_only=88dfef31462a41bcac8beef69e062193) in Supplementary S1.
text.formatted: Detailed descriptions are publicly available online (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/47z8a/overview?view_only=88dfef31462a41bcac8beef69e062193">https://osf.io/47z8a/overview?view_only=88dfef31462a41bcac8beef69e062193</ref>) in Supplementary S1.

text.text: Each participant completed 13 sessions corresponding to different audio conditions, with each session explicitly conducted on a separate day.
This strictly distributed daily scheduling ensured a minimum 24-hour washout period between exposures, rigorously precluding any autonomic carry-over effects or physiological habituation.
Sessions were scheduled flexibly across mornings, afternoons, or evenings, depending on participant availability, with the overall experimental flow illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Sessions were scheduled flexibly across mornings, afternoons, or evenings, depending on participant availability, with the overall experimental flow illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1</ref>.

text.text: At each session, participants first rested quietly for three minutes, after which baseline cardiovascular measurements were obtained.
They then listened to a brief guided breathing meditation audio while biosignals were continuously recorded.
Post-intervention cardiovascular measurements were collected immediately afterward.

Following each session, participants completed self-report questionnaires in approximately 3-5 minutes, whereas the health status assessment and demographic questionnaire were required only at the first session.
The order of audio presentation was randomized for each participant.
Counseling contact information was provided upon completion of the study.

The intervention materials were derived from the Official YouTube Channel of Dharma Drum Mountain (DDM), an openly available channel (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AVHgF3TQoV8), an educational non-profit organization with extensive expertise in Chinese Chan meditation and contemplative training.
text.formatted: The intervention materials were derived from the Official YouTube Channel of Dharma Drum Mountain (DDM), an openly available channel (<ref type="url" target="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AVHgF3TQoV8">https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AVHgF3TQoV8</ref>), an educational non-profit organization with extensive expertise in Chinese Chan meditation and contemplative training.

text.text: DDM's Chan-based system emphasizes mind training and the systematic cultivation of attentional regulation and metacognitive awareness.

Its meditation pedagogy follows a structured and progressive practice map, typically advancing from introductory instruction to foundational attentional training and then to more intensive retreat-based formats.
The 4-min-5-s breathing guidance audio was excerpted and adapted from an open-access Breath Chan video produced by the Dharma Drum Mountain Official Channel (2021).
The original recording was released during the COVID-19 lockdown and was intended for the general public, including individuals without Buddhist or religious affiliation.
To minimize contextual content unrelated to the breathing practice itself, the introductory and concluding segments related to pandemic-specific mental health promotion were removed.
The core instructional content was retained, and the audio was regenerated with systematic modifications to pitch and sound characteristics.
The resulting audio incorporated natural ambient sounds and consisted of two guided phases, namely phase 1 (p1: 0-120 s) and phase 2 (p2: 120-245 s), delivered in Mandarin Chinese.

In phase 1, participants were instructed to close their eyes, shift attention to bodily sensations, refrain from deliberate thinking, gently move their shoulders up and down to release tension, relax their abdomens, and rest in a relaxed state.
This phase functioned as a brief bodyscanning practice.

In phase 2, participants were guided to focus attention on the tip of the nose and observe natural, voluntary breathing while silently counting breaths, thereby engaging in a breathing-focused practice.
The transcript and audio files for the breathing guidance are available online in Supplementary S2.
Based on the original breathing-guidance content, 13 audio variants were generated to examine how acoustic differences might relate to physiological responses.

Thirteen breathing-meditation audio files were created to represent combinations of pitch, speaker identity, and background natural sound, yielding the following labels: F, Fl, Fh, M, Ml, Mh, N, FN, FlN, FhN, MN, MlN, and MhN.
All files were batch-processed in MATLAB (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022k) using built-in and toolbox functions.
Audio was read using the "audioread" function (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022a).
Stereo files were converted to mono by averaging channels.
No amplitude normalization or denoising was applied to the waveform prior to feature extraction.
Acoustic features were computed from the full waveform and short-time frames.

Zerocrossing rate (ZCR) was computed over the entire signal as the number of times the amplitude crossed the zero axis and was commonly used as a coarse descriptor of noisiness or unvoiced content (Bachu et al., 2010; Mitrović et al., 2010; Rabiner & Schafer, 2007).
text.formatted: Zerocrossing rate (ZCR) was computed over the entire signal as the number of times the amplitude crossed the zero axis and was commonly used as a coarse descriptor of noisiness or unvoiced content <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bachu et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mitrović et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rabiner & Schafer, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For frame-based spectral features, signals were segmented into 30-ms frames with 15-ms overlap and multiplied by a Hamming window ("Hamming" function, Oppenheim, 1999).
text.formatted: For frame-based spectral features, signals were segmented into 30-ms frames with 15-ms overlap and multiplied by a Hamming window ("Hamming" function, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oppenheim, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Spectral centroid and spectral spread were computed per frame using the magnitude spectrum as weights and then averaged across frames to yield file-level summaries.

Spectral centroid was defined as the magnitude-weighted mean frequency, whereas spectral spread was defined as the magnitude-weighted root-mean-square deviation from the spectral centroid, also called bandwidth (Mitrović et al., 2010; Tzanetakis & Cook, 2002).
text.formatted: Spectral centroid was defined as the magnitude-weighted mean frequency, whereas spectral spread was defined as the magnitude-weighted root-mean-square deviation from the spectral centroid, also called bandwidth <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mitrović et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tzanetakis & Cook, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs; 13 coefficients with log energy appended) were extracted with the same framing parameters using the "mfcc" function (Rabiner & Schafer, 2011), which processes the audio signal via a fast Fourier transform, a Mel-scale filterbank approximating human nonlinear auditory perception, logarithmic compression of filterbank energies, and a discrete cosine transform (DCT; Mitrović et al., 2010; Rabiner & Schafer, 2007).
text.formatted: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs; 13 coefficients with log energy appended) were extracted with the same framing parameters using the "mfcc" function <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rabiner & Schafer, 2011)</ref>, which processes the audio signal via a fast Fourier transform, a Mel-scale filterbank approximating human nonlinear auditory perception, logarithmic compression of filterbank energies, and a discrete cosine transform (DCT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mitrović et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rabiner & Schafer, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Fundamental frequency (F0) was estimated using MATLAB's "pitch" function (Atal, 1972;  The Mathworks, Inc., 2022g) with the default search range (50-400 Hz). This range reflects typical adult voice fundamentals, which were generally <400 Hz and well above very low noise frequencies in voiced speech (Pisanski et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Fundamental frequency (F0) was estimated using MATLAB's "pitch" function <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Atal, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> The Mathworks, Inc., 2022g) with the default search range (50-400 Hz). This range reflects typical adult voice fundamentals, which were generally <400 Hz and well above very low noise frequencies in voiced speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Pisanski et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Pitch estimates were screened to remove NaNs prior to computing the mean and standard deviation.

For descriptive visualization and quality control, linear-frequency spectrograms ("spectrograms" function; Boualem Boashash, 2015; Fulop & Fitz, 2006; Hlawatsch & Auger, 2013; Oppenheim, 1999; Rabiner & Schafer, 1978a) were generated using a 20-ms window with 10-ms overlap.
text.formatted: For descriptive visualization and quality control, linear-frequency spectrograms ("spectrograms" function; Boualem Boashash, 2015; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fulop & Fitz, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hlawatsch & Auger, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oppenheim, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rabiner & Schafer, 1978a)</ref> were generated using a 20-ms window with 10-ms overlap.

text.text: Mel-spectrograms ("melSpectrogram" function; O'Shaughnessy, 1987; Rabiner & Schafer, 2011; Søndergaard & Majdak, 2013) were computed using a 20-ms Hamming window with 10-ms overlap (64 mel bands; FFT length set to the next power of two of the window length).
text.formatted: Mel-spectrograms ("melSpectrogram" function; O'Shaughnessy, 1987; Rabiner & Schafer, 2011; Søndergaard & Majdak, 2013) were computed using a 20-ms Hamming window with 10-ms overlap (64 mel bands; FFT length set to the next power of two of the window length).

text.text: Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated from the full waveform using Welch's method "pwelch" (Hayes, 1996; Stoica et al., 2005) with a Hann window length (Oppenheim, 1999) equal to the signal length and plotted from 0 to 𝐹 !
text.formatted: Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated from the full waveform using Welch's method "pwelch" <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hayes, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stoica et al., 2005)</ref> with a Hann window length <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Oppenheim, 1999)</ref> equal to the signal length and plotted from 0 to 𝐹 !

text.text: /2Hz.
To quantify similarity among the 13 files, ZCR, spectral centroid, spectral spread, MFCC (14 dimensions), and pitch statistics were combined into a feature matrix.
Files with missing values were excluded listwise.
Pairwise Euclidean distances were computed on z-scored features using the "pdist" function (Dattorro, 2010; Hadsell et al., 2006; Song et al., 2016) and visualized as a heatmap.
text.formatted: Pairwise Euclidean distances were computed on z-scored features using the "pdist" function <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dattorro, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hadsell et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Song et al., 2016)</ref> and visualized as a heatmap.

text.text: Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted using the "pca" function (Ilin & Raiko, 2010; Jackson, 2005; Jolliffe, 2002; Krzanowski, 1988; Roweis, 1997; Seber, 2004), which mean-centered the feature matrix and extracted principal components and explained variance to characterize low-dimensional structure among the audio files.
text.formatted: Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted using the "pca" function <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ilin & Raiko, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Jackson, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Jolliffe, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Krzanowski, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Roweis, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Seber, 2004)</ref>, which mean-centered the feature matrix and extracted principal components and explained variance to characterize low-dimensional structure among the audio files.

text.text: Feature standardization was applied only at the feature-matrix level and did not affect the original audio signals or frame-level acoustic measures.

This study employed using the Mind Media NeXus-10 MKII to record blood volume pulse (BVP), respiration (RSP), electrodermal activity (EDA), and skin temperature (Temp) during brief breathing meditation across 13 audio conditions.
Pulse rate variability (PRV) was derived from BVP signals sampled at 128 Hz, whereas RSP, EDA, and TEMP were recorded at 32 Hz.
All signals were exported at 1028 Hz and subsequently downsampled and preprocessed using MATLAB's Data Cleaner and Signal Analyzer applications (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022i, 2022b).
Signal preprocessing included artifact detection, filtering, and denoising, with parameter settings summarized in Supplementary S3.
Biosignal features were then extracted separately for each audio condition and guidance phase, namely phase 1 (p1: 0-120 s) and phase 2 (p2: 120-245 s).
Pulse rate variability (PRV) indices were derived from the preprocessed BVP signal.

Within each phase and audio condition, the BVP waveform was low-pass filtered at 7 Hz using a fifth-order Butterworth filter with zero-phase forward-backward filtering ("butter" and "filtfilt" functions; Gustafsson, 1996; Lyons, Richard G, 2004; Mitra, Sanjit K, 2001; Oppenheim, 1999).
text.formatted: Within each phase and audio condition, the BVP waveform was low-pass filtered at 7 Hz using a fifth-order Butterworth filter with zero-phase forward-backward filtering ("butter" and "filtfilt" functions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Gustafsson, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lyons, Richard G, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mitra, Sanjit K, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oppenheim, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: A Hilbert transform was then applied to obtain the analytic signal, and the amplitude envelope was computed as the absolute value ("Hilbert" function; Claerbout, Jon F, 1985; Marple, 1999; Oppenheim, 1999).
text.formatted: A Hilbert transform was then applied to obtain the analytic signal, and the amplitude envelope was computed as the absolute value ("Hilbert" function; <ref type="bibr">Claerbout, Jon F, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Marple, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oppenheim, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Peaks were identified on the envelope using MATLAB's "findpeaks" function (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022c).
To restrict detections to physiologically plausible pulse rates, the minimum inter-peak distance was set to correspond to a maximum heart rate of 200 beats/min.

The minimum peak prominence was defined using a data-adaptive rule based on global envelope statistics, namely the larger of a fixed fraction of the median envelope amplitude and a fixed fraction of its 20-80% inter-percentile range.
This thresholding rule was applied uniformly across recordings to suppress low-amplitude noise peaks while preserving physiologically plausible pulses.
Signal waveforms are reported in Figure 3 and Supplementary S4.

text.text: Pulse intervals (PP intervals) were calculated as the time differences between successive detected peaks and converted to milliseconds.
PP intervals outside the physiological range of 300-2000 ms, corresponding to 30-200 beats/min, were excluded from subsequent analyses.

Among physiologically plausible intervals, those deviating by more than 50% from a sevenbeat moving median were flagged for quality-control summaries, whereas all intervals within the physiological range were retained for the main PRV computations.
No interpolation or local average correction was applied.

Consistent with HRV/PRV recording-duration conventions, 5-min recordings are generally considered short-term, whereas recordings shorter than 5 min are typically described as ultrashort-term (Electrophysiology, 1996; Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017).
text.formatted: Consistent with HRV/PRV recording-duration conventions, 5-min recordings are generally considered short-term, whereas recordings shorter than 5 min are typically described as ultrashort-term <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Electrophysiology, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For each participant, audio condition, and phase, mean pulse rate (PR, bpm; ≥5 valid intervals and ≥5 s of data) and time-domain pulse rate variability (PRV) indices were computed when sufficient data were available (≥30 valid intervals and ≥20 s of data).

Time domain PRV indices included the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD, ms) and the standard deviation of successive differences (SDSD, ms), both derived from PP-interval series after physiological screening.
Ultra-short-term variability was quantified using the Poincaré plot index SD1 (ms), calculated from the dispersion of successive PP interval pairs.
SD1 divided by RMSSD (SD1/RMSSD) was further calculated as an indicator of baroreceptor function.

In addition, beat-wise BVP amplitude was defined as the difference between the filtered BVP value at each detected peak and the minimum filtered BVP value in the interval between that peak and the subsequent peak.
The mean of these beat-wise amplitudes within each analysis phase was used as an index of overall pulse amplitude, serving as a proxy for relative microvascular pulse expansion at the recording site.

Linear slope of BVP amplitude was summarized by a linear trend estimated via first-order ordinary least squares regression of beat-wise amplitude on time using MATLAB's "polyfit" function with degree 1, with the slope coefficient retained as the rate of amplitude change over time (Electrophysiology, 1996
text.formatted: Linear slope of BVP amplitude was summarized by a linear trend estimated via first-order ordinary least squares regression of beat-wise amplitude on time using MATLAB's "polyfit" function with degree 1, with the slope coefficient retained as the rate of amplitude change over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Electrophysiology, 1996</ref>

text.text: Respiratory indices were computed from the preprocessed respiration signal.

Within each analysis phase and audio condition, candidate inspiratory peaks and expiratory troughs were identified in the time domain using "islocalmax" and "islocalmin" functions (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022f, 2022e), respectively, with a minimum separation of 2 s (64 samples) to limit spurious detections driven by residual high-frequency fluctuations and to remain consistent with an upper bound of approximately 30 breaths/min.
Respiratory cycles were then defined using a peak centered, structure preserving pairing procedure that enforced a trough-peak-trough sequence.
For each detected peak, the nearest preceding trough and nearest subsequent trough were located, and cycles were retained only when a valid ordering (trough < peak < trough) was present.
text.formatted: For each detected peak, the nearest preceding trough and nearest subsequent trough were located, and cycles were retained only when a valid ordering (trough < peak < trough) was present.

text.text: Inspiratory time (TI) and expiratory time (TE) were computed as the sample-count differences between paired events and converted to seconds using the sampling rate.
The inter-breath interval (IBI) was defined as the trough-to-trough duration of each constructed cycle.

To restrict analyses to physiologically plausible breathing and reduce event-mispairing artifacts, cycles were screened by requiring IBI to fall within 2-12 s, corresponding to 5-30 breaths/min, and by constraining TI and TE to occupy a reasonable proportion of the corresponding cycle length (0.2-0.8 of IBI).
Respiratory rate (RR, bpm) was summarized as 60 divided by the mean IBI to maintain consistency with cycle timing.
For each participant, audio condition, and phase, mean RR, mean IBI, mean TI, mean TE, and the mean inspiratory-to-expiratory ratio (I:E = mean TI / mean TE) were derived from retained cycles.

A relative respiration amplitude metric was computed per cycle as the difference between the signal value at each detected peak and its immediately preceding trough, and the mean amplitude was used as an index of within-signal peak-to-trough excursion (Grassmann et al., 2016; Van Den Bosch et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A relative respiration amplitude metric was computed per cycle as the difference between the signal value at each detected peak and its immediately preceding trough, and the mean amplitude was used as an index of within-signal peak-to-trough excursion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Grassmann et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Van Den Bosch et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: PR Max-Min difference was quantified as a time-domain index of RespPRV derived from the joint analysis of preprocessed BVP and RSP signals.
Instantaneous PR was obtained using the same BVP preprocessing and PP-interval screening pipeline described in the BVP section.

Accordingly, RespPRV estimation relied on the same peak detection, physiological screening, and interval transformation logic as the main PRV analysis, ensuring comparability across cardiac-derived indices.
Instantaneous PR (bpm) was computed as 60 divided by each retained PP interval and indexed to the corresponding interval-end timestamps.

To reduce instability from extremely sparse PP-interval series, RespPRV estimation was attempted only when the BVP-derived interval series provided at least 5 retained intervals spanning at least 5 s.
Respiratory cycles were defined within each analysis phase using the same event detection and cycle construction procedure reported in the RSP section.

The irregularly time-stamped instantaneous PR series was resampled to a uniform 4-Hz grid using piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation ("interp1" function with pchip; Fritsch & Carlson, 1980; Kahaner et al., 1988; San Roman et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The irregularly time-stamped instantaneous PR series was resampled to a uniform 4-Hz grid using piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation ("interp1" function with pchip; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fritsch & Carlson, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kahaner et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">San Roman et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Resampling was performed only over the time window in which RSP data within each phase and the BVP-derived PR series were both available.
Cases with minimal temporal overlap were not carried forward.

Within each retained trough-to-trough respiratory cycle, resampled PR values were queried to obtain the within-cycle maximum and minimum, and PR max -PR min (bpm; Elstad et al., 2018; Menuet et al., 2025; Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017) was computed on a breath-by-breath basis.
text.formatted: Within each retained trough-to-trough respiratory cycle, resampled PR values were queried to obtain the within-cycle maximum and minimum, and PR max -PR min (bpm; Elstad et al., 2018; Menuet et al., 2025; Shaffer & Ginsberg, 2017) was computed on a breath-by-breath basis.

text.text: Phase-level summaries were produced only when each contributing respiratory cycle contained at least 2 non-missing resampled PR samples within the trough-to-trough window and when at least 3 qualifying cycles contributed to the phase estimate.

text.text: Electrodermal activity (EDA; also termed galvanic skin response, GSR) was measured as skin conductance (SC) using two finger electrodes placed on palmar sites to index sympathetic arousal driven by limbic-system activation of eccrine sweat glands in the palms (Braithwaite et  Prior to cvxEDA decomposition, phase-level data integrity was screened; phases with insufficient finite samples were excluded, and remaining non-finite values were linearly interpolated using MATLAB's "interp1" function (linear; extrap; The Mathworks, Inc., 2022).

text.text: SCL was summarized as the mean of the cvxEDA tonic component, which operationalized SCL as the sustained conductance background.

Cumulative phasic activity was quantified as the area under the curve (AUC) of the half-wave-rectified cvxEDA phasic component, 𝑟positive = max (𝑟,0), computed by numerical integration ("trapz" function; The Mathworks, Inc., 2022) and divided by the sampling rate to express AUC in μS•s (Benedek & Kaernbach, 2010; Greco et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Cumulative phasic activity was quantified as the area under the curve (AUC) of the half-wave-rectified cvxEDA phasic component, 𝑟positive = max (𝑟,0), computed by numerical integration ("trapz" function; The Mathworks, Inc., 2022) and divided by the sampling rate to express AUC in μS•s <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benedek & Kaernbach, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Greco et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Phasic AUC was additionally normalized by the realized phase duration to yield a duration-adjusted index (μS) for comparisons across phases with slightly different usable lengths.
The primary goal of the EDA analysis was to quantify how analysis phases and audio conditions influenced overall SC, focusing on SCL and phasic AUC.

text.text: Finger skin temperature (°C) was recorded from the left index finger as a peripheral measure influenced by thermoregulatory processes, including cutaneous blood flow and eccrine sweating (Cramer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Finger skin temperature (°C) was recorded from the left index finger as a peripheral measure influenced by thermoregulatory processes, including cutaneous blood flow and eccrine sweating <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cramer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Temperature features were computed separately for each participant, audio condition, and phase.
Missing samples were removed together with their timestamps, and no interpolation or gap-filling was applied.
Within each predefined phase and audio condition, two indices were computed.
Mean peripheral skin temperature was calculated as the arithmetic average of all retained samples within the phase.

Temporal change in temperature was summarized by first-order ordinary least squares regression of temperature on time using MATLAB's polyfit function (The Mathworks, Inc., 2022h), with the slope coefficient retained as the rate of temperature change (°C/s).
To improve numerical conditioning without altering the slope estimate, time values were mean-centered within each fitted phase window prior to model fitting.
When fewer than two valid samples were available within a phase, the slope estimate was recorded as missing.
Likewise, when a phase contained no valid samples, phase-specific features were recorded as missing.
The linear trend was used as a parsimonious descriptive summary of within-phase temperature change over time.

text.text: Pre-and post-intervention systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and pulse rate (PR) were measured using an Omron HEM-1000 upper arm blood pressure monitor while participants were seated with both feet flat on the floor.

Measurements were obtained from the left upper arm and were available during morning sessions (8:30 a.m.-12:00 p.m.), afternoon sessions (12:01 p.m.-6:00 p.m.), and evening sessions (6:01 p.m.-10:00 p.m.), depending on participant availability.
Participants completed the following self-report measures.

The Audio Feeling Scale and the Taiwanese Daily Stress Inventory (TDSI) were completed after each session, whereas the health status assessment and demographic questionnaire were completed only at the first session.

Participants completed two single-item assessments of health status using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very poor to5 = excellent): (1) "Over the past month, how would you rate your psychological health?"
and (2) "Over the past month, how would you rate your physical health?"
Both items were included in the demographic questionnaire.
Daily minor stress over the past 24 hours was assessed using the TDSI (Chang & Yao, 2025), adapted from the Daily Stress Inventory (DSI; Brantley et al., 1987).
text.formatted: Daily minor stress over the past 24 hours was assessed using the TDSI (Chang & Yao, 2025), adapted from the Daily Stress Inventory (DSI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brantley et al., 1987)</ref>.

text.text: The measure comprises 58 items rated from 1 to 7, with non-occurring events scored as 0.
Three indices were derived: the frequency of stressful events (FREQ), the total impact score (SUM), and the average impact rating (AIR = SUM/FREQ).

Consistent with the original DSI report (Brantley et al., 1987), internal consistency was summarized for FREQ and SUM in the present sample (Cronbach's α = .80, 95% CI [.77, .83] for FREQ; α = .84, 95% CI [.80, .88] for SUM).

text.text: TDSI scores were used to descriptively characterize daily stress prior to each session.
Statistical analyses were conducted in JASP 0.95.4 (JASP Team, 2025), and audio and biosignal processing was performed in MATLAB R2022b (The MathWorks Inc., 2022).
Descriptive statistics were computed for demographics, health-related, and meditation-related characteristics.
Questionnaire reliability was assessed with Cronbach's α, with values ≥ .80 indicating acceptable internal consistency (Cheung et al., 2024).

text.text: To characterize the acoustic structure of the 13 audio conditions, ZCR, spectral centroid, spectral spread, MFCC-derived features, and pitch statistics were summarized and entered into similarity analyses.
Pairwise Euclidean distances were computed on z-scored acoustic features, and principal component analysis (PCA) was used to characterize the low-dimensional structure of the audio conditions.

Given the high-dimensional nature of the acoustic feature matrix and multiparametric biosignals, our correlational analyses were treated as exploratory feature engineering to map the bioacoustic landscape, identifying primary candidate parameters for future confirmatory trials.
For cardiovascular outcomes, repeated-measures ANOVAs were used to examine changes in SBP, DBP, and PR across audio groups.
For phase-based biosignal analyses, 2 × 3 repeatedmeasures ANOVAs were conducted with phase (phase 1 [p1], phase 2 [p2]) and audio group (H, N, HN) as within-subject factors.
Type III sums of squares were used.
Sphericity was evaluated using Mauchly's test, and Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied when ε < .75, whereas Huynh-Feldt corrections were applied when ε ≥ .75.
text.formatted: Sphericity was evaluated using Mauchly's test, and Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied when ε < .75, whereas Huynh-Feldt corrections were applied when ε ≥ .75.

text.text: Effect sizes were reported as omega squared (ω²) and generalized eta squared (η²G).
Statistical significance was set at p < .05. (Blanca et al., 2023; Huynh & Feldt, 1976; Olejnik & Algina, 2003).

text.text: Pearson's correlation analyses were conducted in two sets.

First, correlations among biosignal indices were examined separately within each audio group × phase combination (H_p1, H_p2, N_p1, N_p2, HN_p1, and HN_p2) to identify condition-specific physiological associations.
Second, correlations were computed across the full audio epoch, without phase separation, to examine associations among biosignal indices, subjective audio feeling, and acoustic features.
All variables were continuous, and all tests were two-tailed.
Significance was defined as p < .05.

text.text: To characterize daily stress during the 24 hours preceding each audio session, TDSI scores were summarized descriptively.
Mean FREQ was 17.07 (SD = 6.45), mean SUM was 43.47 (SD = 21.22), and mean AIR was 2.52 (SD = 0.74).

PCA demonstrated a clear separation between natural sounds and human voices along the first two principal components based on variations in acoustic features, classifying the 13 audio files into three clusters: (a) human voice with pitch variation (H), (b) human voice with pitch variation and natural sound (HN), and (c) natural sound only (N).

Pairwise Euclidean distances further showed that the natural sound stimulus was acoustically distinct from all human voice recordings, whereas voices differing in biological sex but sharing similar pitch and background ambiance were the most similar.
The natural sound file (N) exhibited the highest ZCR among the 13 audio stimuli, reflecting a higher frequency of signal polarity changes.

text.text: Voice containing and natural sound conditions showed both recurrent and audio group specific physiological coupling patterns.
Across audio groups and phases, several stable recurrent associations emerged (Table 1).
text.formatted: Across audio groups and phases, several stable recurrent associations emerged (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The most consistent finding was that greater PR max-PR min was associated with greater PRV across all audio groups in both phases.
Higher PR was also associated with lower PRV in most conditions, except HN during phase 2.
Larger BVP amplitude was repeatedly associated with higher peripheral skin temperature, except in HN during phase 2.

In addition, greater PR max-PR min was consistently associated with slower and longer breathing in the voicecontaining conditions (H and HN) across both phases, but not in the natural-sound condition.
Together, these findings indicate partially stable coupling among RespPRV, PRV, PR, and peripheral skin temperature across changes in phase and audio context.
Phase-specific and audio group -specific physiological coupling patterns were observed across electrodermal, vascular, respiratory, and PRV indices.
In phase 1, greater phasic electrodermal activity was associated with higher SCL across audio groups.
In the two-voice containing conditions, greater PR max -PR min was additionally associated with lower SCL, and larger BVP amplitude was associated with lower PRV.

At the level of individual audio groups, slower respiration in H was associated with lower phasic electrodermal activity, including longer IBI (r = -.438, p = .047) and longer TE (r = -.462, p = .035).

In N, a greater positive slope of BVP amplitude was associated with lower PRV, including RMSSD, SD1, and SDSD (r = -.530 to -.529, p = .014), and with lower peripheral skin temperature (r = -.542, p = .011).
In HN, larger BVP amplitude was associated with greater phasic electrodermal activity (r = .555, p = .009) but lower PR max -PR min (r = -.579, p = .006).
Phase 2-specific patterns further differentiated the three audio groups.
In H, a greater positive slope of BVP amplitude was associated with higher PRV, including RMSSD, SD1, and SDSD (r = .446, p = .043), and with greater PR max -PR min (r = .578, p = .006).

In N, phasic electrodermal activity was inversely associated with SCL (r = -.566, p = .007) and peripheral skin temperature (r = -.439, p = .047), whereas SCL was positively associated with peripheral skin temperature (r = .499, p = .021).
In HN, both the slope and mean level of BVP amplitude were strongly positively associated with phasic electrodermal activity (r = .909-.980, p < .001).
text.formatted: In HN, both the slope and mean level of BVP amplitude were strongly positively associated with phasic electrodermal activity (r = .909-.980, p < .001).

text.text: Physiological couplings were partly stable across phases, yet some were reorganized or even reversed depending on the audio context.
Several associations were also preserved across both phases within the human voice condition (H).

Larger BVP amplitude remained associated with PRV across both phases (r = -.436 to-.546, p = .010 to .048), greater phasic electrodermal activity remained associated with higher SCL (phase 1: r = .686, p < .001; phase 2: r = .791, p < .001), and greater PR max -PR min remained associated with longer IBI (r = .531 to .752 p = <.001 to .013) and longer TE and TI (r = .440 to .716, p = <.001 to .046).

text.text: Several associations were also preserved across both phases within HN.

Larger mean BVP amplitude remained associated with greater phasic electrodermal activity (r = .555 to .909, p = < .001 to .009) but lower PR max -PR min (r = -.449 to -.579, p = .006 to .041) across both phases.
text.formatted: Larger mean BVP amplitude remained associated with greater phasic electrodermal activity (r = .555 to .909, p = < .001 to .009) but lower PR max -PR min (r = -.449 to -.579, p = .006 to .041) across both phases.

text.text: The HN condition also showed inverse associations of PRV with SCL (r = -.444 to -.516, p = .017 to .044) and peripheral skin temperature (phase 1: r = -.483 to -.501, p = .021 to .026), as well as of PR max -PR min with SCL (r = -.446 to -.472, p = .031 to .043).
Phase-related reversals were also observed.
In N, phasic electrodermal activity was positively associated with SCL in phase 1 (r = .609, p = .003), but negatively in phase 2 (r = -.566, p = .007).

A similar reversal was observed in HN for the association between the slope of BVP amplitude and phasic electrodermal activity, which was negative in phase 1 (r = -.613, p = .003) but strongly positive in phase 2 (r = .980, p < .001).
text.formatted: A similar reversal was observed in HN for the association between the slope of BVP amplitude and phasic electrodermal activity, which was negative in phase 1 (r = -.613, p = .003) but strongly positive in phase 2 (r = .980, p < .001).

text.text: These reversals suggest that some physiological couplings were not merely strengthened or weakened over time, but qualitatively reorganized across phases depending on audio context.

text.text: Subjective audio feeling did not differ significantly across audio groups (F(1.364, 27.288) = .258, p = .689) for the full audio.
Nevertheless, several acoustic features were associated with BVP-derived indices.

In particular, the BVP amplitude slope, PR, PRV indices, and PR max-PR min showed consistent associations with ZCR (r = -.182, p = .002), spectral centroid (r = -.196, p = .001), spectral spread (r = -.121 to -.243, p = <.001 to .045), pitch (r = -.205 to -.126, p = <.001 to .037), log energy (r = -.127 to -.216, p = <.001 to .036), and multiple MFCC components (r = -.196 to .365, p = <.001 to .046).
text.formatted: In particular, the BVP amplitude slope, PR, PRV indices, and PR max-PR min showed consistent associations with ZCR (r = -.182, p = .002), spectral centroid (r = -.196, p = .001), spectral spread (r = -.121 to -.243, p = <.001 to .045), pitch (r = -.205 to -.126, p = <.001 to .037), log energy (r = -.127 to -.216, p = <.001 to .036), and multiple MFCC components (r = -.196 to .365, p = <.001 to .046).

text.text: Electrodermal and temperature-related indices also showed selective acoustic associations.

Phasic electrodermal activity was only associated with MFCC 11 (r = -.135, p = .026), whereas SCL, peripheral skin temperature, and temperature slope were associated with a broader set of acoustic features, including ZCR (r = -.164 to .304, p = <.001 t o.021), spectral centroid (r = -.157 to .300, p = <.001 t o.020), spectral spread (r = -.140 to .228, p = <.001 t o.021), pitch (r = -.162 to .318, p = <.001 t o.007), and selected MFCC components (r = -.164 to .158, p = .006 to .021).

Although subjective audio feeling did not differ by audio group, it was still associated with several acoustic features, particularly mean pitch (r = .161, p =.008) and selected MFCC components (r = -.198 to .217, p = <.001 to .046).

text.text: The present study provides unprecedented psychophysiological evidence that the acoustic properties of audio-guided interventions act as independent, potent modulators of human autonomic dynamics.

Consistent with recent evidence that short-term structured respiration practices can modify respiratory physiology, particularly respiratory rate (Balban et al., 2023), the present findings further showed that ultra-short-term respiratory dynamics were sensitive to the acoustic context of guided breathing.
text.formatted: Consistent with recent evidence that short-term structured respiration practices can modify respiratory physiology, particularly respiratory rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Balban et al., 2023)</ref>, the present findings further showed that ultra-short-term respiratory dynamics were sensitive to the acoustic context of guided breathing.

text.text: Respiratory rate and inspiratory time varied across audio groups, and respiratory rate, expiratory time, and inter-breath interval showed phase-by-audio-group interactions.

In contrast, systemic blood pressure showed a generalized pre-post reduction that did not depend on audio group, suggesting that the cardiovascular effect reflected a broad response to brief guided breathing, whereas respiratory dynamics were more selectively shaped by acoustic context.
This confirms that the fundamental cognitive task of maintaining a spontaneous natural pattern of breath awareness is highly robust against structural acoustic changes.
However, beneath this generalized cardiovascular reduction, our high-resolution multiparametric analyses unmasked a highly modular, acoustically driven physiological architecture.
Crucially, we demonstrated that different physiological systems tune into distinct dimensions of the digital audio stimulus.
Macro-level respiratory indices, such as respiratory rate and inspiratory time, were primarily driven by the broad categorical nature of the sound (e.g., human voice versus natural ambiance).

In stark contrast, micro-level autonomic tonespecifically electrodermal activity and pulse rate variability-exhibited profound sensitivity to fine-grained computational acoustic features, including the zero-crossing rate, spectral centroid, and specific Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs).
This aligns with advanced bioacoustic frameworks (Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2022) suggesting that MFCCs and spectral features capture subtle, arousal-related acoustic frequencies.
text.formatted: This aligns with advanced bioacoustic frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Wang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Zhao et al., 2022)</ref> suggesting that MFCCs and spectral features capture subtle, arousal-related acoustic frequencies.

text.text: These frequencies can bypass conscious cognitive processing to directly innervate peripheral microvascular and eccrine responses.
The acoustic stimulus is therefore not a neutral instructional medium; it is an active, programmable exogenous physiological trigger.

Furthermore, our intensive 13-condition within-subject design allowed us to observe that physiological coupling-such as the complex interplay between blood volume pulse amplitude and phasic skin conductance-reorganizes dynamically based on the specific acoustic context.

We observed that certain autonomic associations completely reversed their directionality between the body-scan phase and the breath-awareness phase, particularly under the hybrid human voice with natural sound condition.

Such profound, contextdependent autonomic reorganization has been largely invisible in previous between-subject meditation research, highlighting the absolute necessity of evaluating the acoustic context of digital interventions.
Several methodological strengths and considerations must be acknowledged.
The final sample was restricted exclusively to young, healthy, meditation-naïve females.
While this limits immediate broad generalizability to older clinical populations, this demographic homogeneity was a deliberate and necessary scientific control strategy.

Given the high sensitivity of autonomic indices (e.g., PRV and EDA) to biological sex and age-related vascular decay, this strict restriction effectively minimized baseline biological noise, permitting the pure isolation of the acoustic stimulus effects.

Furthermore, while the participant count (N = 21) may appear modest for standard between-subject designs, the rigorous requirement for each participant to return to the laboratory across 13 separate days yielded 273 high-density experimental observations.
This strictly distributed daily scheduling ensured a minimum 24-hour washout period between exposures, rigorously precluding any autonomic carry-over effects or physiological habituation.
This exceptionally demanding repeated-measures approach robustly captured intra-individual physiological coupling dynamics without the confound of same-day autonomic fatigue.
These findings fundamentally challenge the prevailing behavioral assumption that audio guidance is merely a neutral delivery medium.
Instead, we demonstrate that even during a standardized cognitive task, the acoustic essence of the soundscape functions as an active, independent physiological driver.
Aligning perfectly with the Sonic One Health framework (Pijanowski et al., 2025), our results highlight the absolute necessity of evaluating the acoustic context in mind-body interventions.
text.formatted: Aligning perfectly with the Sonic One Health framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Pijanowski et al., 2025)</ref>, our results highlight the absolute necessity of evaluating the acoustic context in mind-body interventions.

text.text: Recognizing that specific acoustic parameters directly drive distinct autonomic reflexes provides objective psychophysiological evidence that soundscapes actively modulate human well-being.

Such next-generation digital therapeutics could dynamically generate and adapt acoustic frequencies in real-time, tailoring the computational acoustic envelope based on a user's momentary physiological feedback, to precisely optimize autonomic downregulation for anxiety, hypertension, and severe stressrelated conditions.

EDA signals were retained in native conductance units (μS) without standardization.

Because EDA integrated both slow baseline drift and faster transient responses, each analysis phase was decomposed using the cvxEDA algorithm (Greco et al., 2016), yielding a tonic component (t) representing skin conductance level (SCL) and a phasic component (r) representing skin conductance responses, and a sparse sympathetic driver (p) of the phasic activity.
To align decomposition with phase-based feature extraction, cvxEDA was applied within each phase using identical settings across all audio conditions.
After each assigned audio condition, participants answered the question, "How did you feel about this audio recording?"
The audio feeling scale was a ten-point emotional icon rating scale to indicate their affective response to the audio.
Following the emoji sentiment analysis of Bai et al. (2019) and Novak et al. (2015), five emoji anchors (😍, 😀, 😶, 😖, 😡) represented positive, neutral, and negative feelings.
Lower scores reflected relaxation or positive affect, whereas higher scores indicated irritation or discomfort.
